Tennessee Fines Caesars Twice, Tired of "Human Error" Excuse

Published October 8, 2026 · 3 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Tennessee's Sports Wagering Advisory Council approved two separate violation agreements against Caesars Sportsbook at its October 6 meeting, fining the operator a combined $4,314.45. The dollar amounts were small, but council members made little effort to hide their frustration with how both violations came about.

College player props that shouldn't have been offered

The first violation surfaced during routine license-renewal research, when Tennessee staff found Caesars had offered prop bets on NCAA baseball — a bet type barred under the state's rules against college player props. Once flagged, a second check turned up the same issue on NCAA volleyball. Combined, the two sports accounted for 118 wagers and roughly $4,900 in handle, and Caesars agreed to a $1,314.45 fine.

Before staff had even finished presenting the details, council chairman Billy Orgel interrupted to tell Caesars' VP of compliance and licensing, Lisa Rankin, that the board was "tired of hearing about human error," likening reliance on manual oversight to running a stock exchange on paper tickets. Council member Hanes Torbett went further, arguing the fine was too small to be worth the state's effort to catch and suggesting a flat, escalating fee any time an operator attributes a violation to "human error." Rankin told the council Caesars had since restricted which employees can modify state-specific betting offerings to prevent a repeat.

A self-exclusion override that let a banned bettor back in

The second violation, raised just after the council believed the Caesars portion of the meeting was finished, was more serious. A bettor who had self-excluded for six months in January opened a second account in February using a different email, phone number, and Social Security number. The automated know-your-customer system correctly blocked the new account — but a Caesars employee manually approved it anyway, checking only that the SSN was a valid format rather than confirming it matched the account holder's identity. That account went on to deposit roughly $3,000 and place 83 wagers before the bettor withdrew winnings. The employee involved was retrained but remains at the company; Caesars agreed to a $3,000 fine.

Why it matters

The episode is a reminder that automated self-exclusion safeguards are only as reliable as the humans who can override them — see our responsible gambling resources for how self-exclusion is supposed to work. It's also a signal worth watching for operators generally: Tennessee's executive director, Mary Beth Thomas, noted that negotiated violation agreements like these save significant staff time compared with a full contested hearing, which is largely why the dollar figures look modest. But with regulators in at least one state now openly impatient with "human error" as a standing explanation, operators leaning on that defense repeatedly may be inviting steeper penalties going forward.
